gravfield.d.M2: Mass 2 (added from the tray) in Earth masses (Moon = 0.0123)
gravfield.d.M3: Mass 3 (added from the tray) in Earth masses
gravfield.d.M4: Mass 4 (added from the tray) in Earth masses
gravfield.d.view: Draw the gravitational field as grid arrows, field lines, or both
gravfield.d.eq: Equipotentials at equal steps $\Delta\Phi$ (dashed) and the one through each point where $g = 0$ (thick, solid)
gravfield.goal.field: Gravitational field: the gravitational force per unit mass on a test mass at each point, $\vec g = \vec F/m$. The field of several masses is the vector sum of the fields of each
gravfield.goal.phi: Gravitational potential $\Phi$ = gravitational potential energy per unit mass, $U/m$ (unit J/kg): $\Phi = -\sum GM_i/r_i$ (zero at infinity). It works like the electric potential $V = U/q$ (Ch 24)
gravfield.goal.grad: $\nabla\Phi$ (the gradient of $\Phi$) points where $\Phi$ rises fastest, with size equal to the rise per unit distance. So $\vec g = -\nabla\Phi$: read the $\Phi$ map as a landscape; $\vec g$ points straight downhill, perpendicular to the equipotential lines, and is larger where they are closer together. The component along a direction is $g_s = -\partial\Phi/\partial s$ (like $E_s = -\partial V/\partial s$ in Ch 24)
gravfield.obs.tray: One mass ($M_1$) to start. Add: drag the disc from the tray at the lower left onto the stage (up to 4); each mass gets its own mass slider in the bar below. Remove: drop a mass on the tray or double tap it (the last one stays). A new mass takes the lowest free number: remove $M_2$, place a new mass, and it is $M_2$ again
gravfield.obs.drag: Drag the masses and the test mass $m$. The thin arrows $\vec g_1, \vec g_2, \dots$ add up to the thick arrow $\vec g$; the numbers are in the Σ panel
gravfield.obs.null: × marks a point where $g = 0$: the fields of the masses add up to zero. With two masses it lies on the line joining them, closer to the lighter one, $r_1/r_2 = \sqrt{M_1/M_2}$ (Earth–Moon: 9.0 : 1, $3.46\times10^5$ km from the Earth)
gravfield.obs.lines: Two kinds of equipotential (legend at the top left). Dashed: $\Phi = -\Delta\Phi, -2\Delta\Phi, \dots$, one per equal step $\Delta\Phi$; the closer together, the stronger the field. Thick solid: a single equipotential drawn at the potential of the × point, whatever the step. Along this line $g$ is not zero; $g = 0$ only at the ×
gravfield.obs.eight: Why the thick line crosses itself at the ×: there $\vec g = -\nabla\Phi = 0$ and the potential has a saddle (highest along the line joining the masses, lowest across it). So it is a figure eight, and it is a boundary: equipotentials inside it enclose each mass separately, those outside enclose both
gravfield.obs.three: Three or more masses: several points where $g = 0$. Three equal masses on an equilateral triangle give four: three saddles near the sides (the thick line crosses itself) and one at the centre. The centre is where the potential is highest within the plane, so its equipotential shrinks to the point (only the × is drawn)
gravfield.obs.perp: Field lines and grid arrows cross the equipotentials at right angles everywhere. Moving along an equipotential, gravity does no work
gravfield.obs.single: One mass (the default): $g \propto 1/r^2$ (twice as far → a quarter of $g$), and the equipotentials are concentric circles whose spacing grows outwards ($\Phi \propto -1/r$)
gravfield.obs.analogy: Compare with the electric field: the same inverse-square law ($F = Gm_1m_2/r^2$ vs $F = k\lvert q_1q_2\rvert/r^2$). Gravity only attracts, so field lines only end on masses (the same shape as an arrangement of negative charges only). As between two like charges, there is a point of zero field between two masses
gravfield.as.units: Length unit $10^5$ km $= 10^8$ m, mass unit the Earth mass $M_\oplus = 5.97\times10^{24}$ kg, $G = 6.674\times10^{-11}\ \mathrm{N\,m^2/kg^2}$ (real values). One Earth mass to start; the default of $M_2$, 0.0123, is the Moon's mass (Earth–Moon distance $3.84\times10^5$ km, mass ratio 81.3)
gravfield.as.point: The masses are fixed point masses (the discs are not to scale; their size grows with the cube root of the mass). The test mass is too small to change the field. $\hat r_i$ is the unit vector from $M_i$ to the point
gravfield.as.plane: The picture is the plane through all the masses: a cut through the 3D inverse-square field. The field is that of masses at rest (orbital motion and its centrifugal effect are not included)
gravfield.as.arrows: Grid arrow length is a log scale of the field strength (over three decades); the direction is exact. The arrows $\vec g_i$ and $\vec g$ at the test mass share a linear scale set by the largest
gravfield.as.eq: Equipotential spacing $\Delta\Phi$: a 1-2-5 step set by the heaviest mass (0.5 MJ/kg for one Earth mass), shown in the legend. The number of field lines is proportional to the mass (24 on the heaviest, at least 1)
gravfield.as.null: The points where $g = 0$ are found numerically (Newton's method, until $|\vec g|$ is below $10^{-13}$ of the sum of the field sizes). All masses lie in this plane, so a zero in the plane is a zero of the 3D field
